rows.title: AUTO BODY REPAIR I
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Analyze, diagnose and apply safe and efficient methods for repairing auto body collision damage
Demonstrate knowledge of characteristics of automotive body repair and apply methods of metalworking procedures as well as those used with automotive plastics and other automotive materials.
Identify different types of vehicle construction, vehicle dimensions, and measuring of vehicles.
Demonstrate safe and efficient welding techniques used in the Auto Body Industry.
objectives: Demonstrate safe and efficient methods for repairing auto body damage.
Demonstrate the operation and maintenance of tools and equipment used to repair auto collision damage.
Demonstrate capacity to measure vehicle dimensions, analyze for damage and determine a plan of action.
Identify, analyze and demonstrate metalworking and filler techniques
Identify, analyze and demonstrate various techniques for repairing plastics and fiberglass panels used in auto body repair.
Identify body panel attachment methods.
Demonstrate the capacity to utilize welding techniques used in auto body repair, including fusion and non-fusion.

rows.title: PHYSICAL ANTHROPOLOGY
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: I am able to demonstrate an understanding of the scientific method
I am able to demonstrate an understanding of cultural traditions in captive and wild ape populations.
I am able to demonstrate and understanding of the processes of fossilization.
I am able to analyze the differences between Anatomically Modern Humans and other hominids.
objectives: Describe the scientific process as a methodology for understanding the natural world, including the steps in the scientific process and the meaning of theory in science.

Define the scope of anthropology and distinguish cultural, archaeology, linguistic and physical anthropology (including dental anthropology, primatology, paleoanthropology, paleopathology, and forensic anthropology).
Identify key historical figures whose concepts provide a foundation for evolutionary theory.
Explain the basic principles of cell structure, DNA, and cell division.
Explain the basic principles of Mendelian and polygenic traits.
Explain the basic principles of modern evolutionary theory (gene flow, mutation, genetic drift and recombination) which produce and distribute genetic variation and the role of natural selection.
Demonstrate an understanding of the classification of living primates: A. Mammalian traits B. Primate physical traits C. Habitats D.Dentition and diet E. Locomotion
Demonstrate an understanding of primate taxonomy: A. Prosimians (lemurs, lorises) B. Tarsiers C. Anthropoids (monkeys, apes and humans) D. Hominoids (apes and humans) E. Hominins

Demonstrate an understanding of nonhuman primate behavior: A. Captive and wild studies B. Dominance hierarchies C. Communication D. Affiliative behavior E. Aggression F. Reproduction G. Mothers and infants H. Cultural behavior I. Human threats J. Primate continuum
Summarize methods used in interpreting the fossil record: A. Processes of fossilization B. Taphonomy C. Relative and chronometric dating techniques

Recognize major groups in nonhuman primate evolutionary history and provide alternate phylogenies: A. Principles of classification B. Vertebrate evolutionary history C. Mammalian evolution D. Miocene fossil hominoids E. Modes of evolutionary change

Recognize major groups of hominin fossils and describe alternate phylogenies for human evolution: A. Definition of hominid B. Bipedal adaptations C. Biocultural evolution D. Paleoanthropology a multidisciplinary approach E. Pre-Australopithecines F. South and East African Australopithecus G. South and East African Paranthropus H. Early Homo I. Taxonomic challenges

Recognize major groups of hominin fossils and describe alternate phylogenies for human evolution (Homo ergaster/erectus and contemporaries): A. Homo ergaster morphology, diet and tool use. B. Homo erectus morphology, diet and tool use. C. Homo georgicus morphology, diet and tool use

Recognize major groups of hominin fossils and describe alternate phylogenies for human evolution (Neandertals and Archaic Homo sapiens): A. Homo heidelbergensis morphology, diet, tool use, and taxonomy B. Neandertal morphology, sites, tool technology, culture, symbolic behavior, diet, burials, genetic evidence

Recognize major groups of hominin fossils and describe alternate phylogenies for human evolution (Homo sapiens): A. Origin and dispersal of anatomically modern humans B. Site locations and estimated ages C. Technology and symbolic expression in Upper Paleolithic

Identify biological and cultural factors responsible for modern human variation and adaptation: A. Concepts of “race” B. Human biocultural evolution C. Population genetics D. Contemporary interpretations of human variation and its adaptive significance E. Impact of infectious disease F. Growth and development (genetics, hormones, environmental factors, cultural factors)
Identify the issues facing humanity: A. Loss of biodiversity B. Overpopulation C. Famine D. Environmental changes

rows.title: ASTRONOMY
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Understand cycles and motions of the sun, moon, stars, and planets.
Describe and explain how light is collected and analyzed in astronomy.
Describe and explain properties and lives of stars and galaxies.
Compare and contrast features of planets and other solar system objects.
Discuss and evaluate astronomy content and value of statements from literature, media, and popular culture.
objectives: Upon completion of this course, the student should be able to: 1. Explain and coordinate systems used in astronomy and how/why each is used: a. longitude and latitude b. altitude and azimuth c. right ascension and declination 2. Describe the motions of the sun and moon as seen from the earth and as seen from outside the earth. 3. Explain the causes of the seasons, the phases of the moon, and the motions of the stars and planets. 4. Use a star chart to recognize astronomical objects and describe the motions of the sun and moon. 5. Explain the difference between and usefulness of sidereal and solar time. 6. Describe the Ptolemaic System. 7. Describe the Copernican System. 8. Explain contributions of certain astronomers. 9. Describe the laws of force, motion and gravitation. 10. Explain the difference between speculation, hypothesis, theories, and observations. 11. Explain the difference between belief in an idea and scientific proof. 12. Describe characteristics of each of the planets and their satellite systems. 13. Describe how to calculate the size of a planet given the distance to the planet and its subtended angle. 14. Calculate various properties of the ellipse. 15. Explain how information is gleaned from the light of distant objects. 16. Explain why stars have different brightnesses. 17. Describe the physical processes occurring inside stars. 18. Explain how we know the distances to some stars. 19. Explain why stars evolve and what they evolve into. 20. Calculate the distances to stars, knowing their apparent and absolute magnitudes. 21. Describe the contents of our Milky Way galaxy and explain how they are related to the galaxy's evolution. 22. Recognize other galaxies and describe their basic properties. 23. Explain the evidence for an expanding universe. 24. Explain the possible origins and fate of the universe.

rows.title: PERSONAL FINANCIAL PLANNING
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Identify personal financial goals and develop strategies to meet those goals.
Analyze various investment options, account types, and other financial tools that can be used to help individuals reach their financial goals.
objectives: Describe the personal financial process and define individual-specific goals. Apply the "time value of money" concepts such as present and future value to put a monetary value on financial goals.
Create a personal balance sheet, income statement and prepare a basic tax return using the appropriate tax forms and rate schedule.
Develop a basic asset management strategy that incorporates establishing a savings plan as well as evaluating alternatives when making major consumer purchases, such as a home or car.
Analyze the reasons for using consumer credit and identify its advantages and disadvantages.
Evaluate personal risk management methods and options for insurance coverage, including life, health, long-term care, disability, home and auto to minimize risk and achieve financial goals.
Describe the role that financial investing plays in the personal financial planning process and identify several different investment objectives.

Summarize the process of buying and selling different financial assets (stocks, bonds, mutual funds, real estate, etc.) and recognize the different types of orders. Identify where to find additional research sources for making such decisions.
Estimate income needs during retirement and create a plan to meet those needs. Identify the role of estate planning, and preparing a will or related document to protect your estate.

rows.title: SMALL GROUP SPEAKING AND COMMUNICATING
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Students will apply the five canons of rhetoric (invention, arrangement, style, memory, and delivery) as the framework for creating and critically evaluating effective speaking through a variety of team presentations.

Students will apply the Aristotelian proofs of ethos, pathos, and logos to creating, delivering, and critically evaluating persuasive oral messages in their speaking activities and team presentations.

Students will find, critically evaluate, and use supporting materials from primary and secondary sources by applying the standards of credibility, including accuracy, relevancy, honesty, transparency, and authority.
Students will demonstrate with their team presentations compelling and engaging arguments tailored to a variety of contexts, audiences, and occasions.
Students will employ organizational patterns of informative and persuasive messages relevant to specific audiences, contexts, and occasions.
Students will demonstrate rhetorical sensitivity to diversity, equity, inclusion, belonging, and accessibility in their team presentations.
Students will demonstrate effective verbal and nonverbal delivery techniques, including methods of managing speaking anxiety.
Students will use critical listening skills to evaluate and provide constructive feedback to their peers and to listen effectively to their fellow group members within a variety of group contexts.
Students will use problem solving methods to create solutions to group problems, including identifying and employing conflict management strategies.
Students will describe how to successfully lead, follow, and motivate diverse group members.
Students will plan and conduct productive group meetings to manage a team project(s).
Students will identify appropriate group communication techniques for specific group situations.
Students will deploy effective verbal and nonverbal communication skills to build group cohesion.
objectives: Employ the five canons of rhetoric (invention, arrangement, style, memory, and delivery) and the Aristotelian proofs of ethos, pathos, and logos, as the framework for creating, delivering, and critically evaluating effective speaking
Find, critically evaluate, and incorporate credible information from primary and secondary sources to support informative and persuasive oral messages.

Formulate and present public messages as a team, and evaluate communication effectiveness through research, analysis, and organization of evidence and visual supporting material appropriate for the audience, occasion, and across a variety of contexts.
Select subject matter, approach, and strategy based on analysis of the communication situation, audience, occasion, and purpose.
Demonstrate compelling and engaging arguments tailored to a variety of contexts, audiences, and occasions.
Employ organizational patterns of informative and persuasive messages relevant to specific audiences, contexts, and occasions
Use effective verbal and nonverbal delivery techniques to deliver effective messages, including use of effective methods of managing communication apprehension.
Identify the psychological, social, and cultural basis and significance of oral communication.
Self-evaluate one's speaking skills of informative and persuasive messages within the team presentation context
Use and evaluate effective problem-solving and decision-making methods.
Demonstrate successful strategies, methods, and skills for managing conflict.
Successfully lead, follow, and motivate diverse group members.
Plan and conduct productive group meetings to manage a team project(s).
Deploy effective verbal and nonverbal communication skills to build group cohesion.
Identify appropriate group communication techniques for specific group situations.
Identify the influences of and communication strategies for ethnic, cultural, generational, gender, and personality diversity.
Identify the strengths and weaknesses of various small group communication theories.
Engage in effective project management skills including managing the group process in pursuit of a shared goal.

Use critical and effective listening skills to evaluate oral presentations, speaking skills, and oral message content (including historical and contemporary public discourse) and to provide constructive feedback to peers in various group situations and settings.
Demonstrate rhetorical and communicative sensitivity to diversity, equity, inclusion, belonging, and accessibility in team presentations and with group communicating.
Adhere to ethical communication practices in team presentations and group communications.

rows.title: ACTING 1
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Formulate a greater comprehension and satisfaction when reading a culturally significant performative text.
Discover the patterns common to most, if not all, dramatic storytelling across cultures.
Practice applying an analytical framework to a selection of a culturally significant play.
Write both personally and academically about the world of drama.
Compose a creative and analytical response to a culturally significant play.
objectives: Demonstrate basic skills of acting, including physical, vocal, imaginative, cultural, analytical, and emotional elements.
Compose a character analysis through a specific cultural lens.
Analyze dramatic textual components as they pertain to interrelationship between the self and the creative arts and of the humanities in a variety of cultures.
Critique a scene from an observer’s point of view, identifying the strengths and weaknesses of that presentation.
Utilize culturally appropriate theatrical terminology and jargon.
Use and apply the basic craft of acting in culturally diverse performance text.

rows.title: PLANE SURVEYING
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Measure and analyze the different types of distances measurements: rectilinear, horizontal, vertical, and sloped
Determine elevations of points using differential leveling data
Conduct closed traverse computations, as well as correcting misclosures
Create and analyze highway, street, and building surveys
Create various types of survey drawings using both hand and computer methods.
Create and analyze horizontal and vertical curves
objectives: Record field notes in a clear, precise, and neat manner.

Measure horizontal and slope distances accurately with an engineer's tape; calculate and determine the tape correction due to changes in tension, changes in temperature, sag, and incorrect horizontal and vertical alignment; explain random errors.
Measure differences in elevation by using a level and the leveling rod, and if necessary be able to correct the error involved in the process.

Demonstrate an understanding of the principles, operations, and adjustments of the transit; use the transit in the field to measure and lay off vertical and horizontal angles and extend lines and other field operations.
Run and adjust a traverse and calculate the area of a traverse.
Measure horizontal and vertical distances by means of a total station.
Develop a topographic map.
Perform calculations involving earthwork, land grading, and horizontal and vertical curves.

rows.title: PHYSICAL GEOGRAPHY
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Identify and describe processes that cause change in the earth's physical environments and ecosystems.

Use the scientific method and tools of geographic analysis, such as maps, globes, charts, and describe remote sensing technologies, Geographic Information Systems (GIS), and Global Positioning Systems (GPS).
Describe the interrelationships between various aspects of the earth's physical environment.
Describe the spatial distribution of the world's major landforms, climates, water bodies, soils, minerals, vegetation ecosystems, and natural resources.
Analyze some of the scientific research on major economic, political, and social implications of the world's physical environment.
objectives: Use the scientific method to study the superficial and atmospheric processes of the earth.
Analyze the interrelationships between various aspects of the earth's physical environment.
Explain the spatial distribution of land forms, water bodies, climates, soils, and vegetation zones.
Analyze the relationship between man and the natural environment.
Apply the scientific method utilizing the tools of geographic research including maps, satellite imagery, and Geographic Information Systems.
Demonstrate an ability to read and interpret maps, and identify locations on the surface of the earth.

rows.title: HEALTH SCIENCE
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Apply discipline based assessment and evaluate strategies to express the credibility and reliability of health literature.
Demonstrate accurate association between food choices, stress, exercise, environmental factors, risk of major non-communicable diseases, and accident prevention
Evaluate lifestyle changes currently made or have plans to make as a result of taking this health education course.
Develop a plan for lifestyle changes that will reduce your risk of major chronic diseases based on your family health history and/or current lifestyle choices.
Describe the dimensions of wellness.
Explain the effects of aging on the dimensions of health.
objectives: Describe the dimensions of wellness (physical, intellectual, psychological, spiritual, social, environmental, and occupational) and their interrelationship.
Distinguish the difference between personal health and public health.

Apply nutrition concepts and dietary recommendations to diet planning throughout the life-cycle and in the promotion of fitness/physical activity, weight management, body composition, and disease prevention.
Identify fitness principles and exercise program components to develop, engage, and improve cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength and endurance, flexibility, and body composition.
Describe the role of stress and mental health in health promotion and disease prevention.
Recognize the stimulus leading to violence and be able to minimize its occurrence.

Describe the role of substance use/abuse/misuse of drugs, including tobacco and alcohol in our society and discuss the short and long term impact to health, treatment, and prevention strategies for individuals, the community, the economy, and the social structure.
Analyze personal and family health as it relates to human sexuality, relationships, sexual orientation, and parenthood.
Identify and discuss specific preventative measures to reduce the risk of various diseases and infections, unintended pregnancies, violence, and addiction.
Examine the physiological, emotional, psychological and sexual aspects of aging.
Describe the inter-relationship between human beings and their environment.
Identify common practices and attitudes that contribute to accidents on a personal and community level and strategies that would reduce their occurrence.
Analyze the health care delivery system, including inequities and discrepancies
Interpret and evaluate health and medical literature information from general and subject specific library and web sources.
Communicate orally and in writing the scientific language of the discipline.
Analyze his/her lifestyle from a wellness perspective. In response, areas of personal behavior change will be identified and ideally, health-enhancing behaviors adopted.

rows.title: MEDICAL ASSISTING BASICS
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Describe the medical assistant scope of practice, role, and responsibilities.
Identify the professional characteristics required of a medical assistant.
objectives: Describe the scope of practice for the medical assistant.
Describe the role and responsibilities of the medical assistant.
Identify the professional characteristics required of the medical assistant.
Describe the process and benefits of certification and registration for the medical assistant.
Apply ethical and legal considerations (principles) to medical assisting practice.
Apply appropriate medical terms and abbreviations used in the medical office.
Apply medical office computer skills.

rows.title: NCLEX PREPARATION
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of the application process for licensure exam (NCLEX).
Apply knowledge from nursing school to analyze NCLEX questions and identify the best answer.
Demonstrate familiarity and increased confidence when taking the NCLEX computerized exam.
objectives: Utilize the nursing process to analyze test questions written in NCLEX format and identify the best answer.
Analyze nursing care and prioritize what action to do first based on client needs.
Verbalize rationale for both correct and incorrect test answers.
Demonstrate familiarity and confidence when taking a computerized test.
Explain the NCLEX test taking process.
Identify self-study needs to prepare for NCLEX exam by reviewing test questions and test scores.

rows.title: PUBLIC HEALTH SCIENCE -  ASPECTS OF DRUG USE
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Describe the effects of drug metabolism, interaction, and use.
Evaluate drug treatment and prevention programs.
Communicate specific drug interactions, legality, and treatment.
Analyze drug use and misuse amongst various socio-cultural constructs including age, gender, and ethnicity.
Relate drug use to major chronic disease.
objectives: Distinguish the difference between drug use, misuse, and abuse as it relates to drug interaction, metabolism, and addiction.
Describe the psychotherapeutic benefits (if any) and harmful effects of common substances of abuse, and identify the populations most at risk of using these substances.

Identify the factors associated with the use of specific substances of abuse, including populations at most risk based on age, sex, education, socioeconomic status, ethnicity, race and age at first initiation.
Apply basic knowledge of drug laws to evaluate historical legal cases and situations related to substance abuse.
Describe the neurological and physiological responses to various types of drugs.
Describe the neurological and physiological short and long term consequences of substance use and abuse including risk of chronic disease.
Analyze the current public health perspective on the issue of substance abuse, including broad political, social and economic factors related to substance abuse.
Interpret reliable public data sources to find statistical and epidemiologic data on incidence, prevalence, and trends in drug, tobacco and alcohol use.
Analyze arguments on both sides of a selected controversial issue, such as drug testing in the work place or legalization of marijuana.
